# Rendering Pipelines and Passes

Also called: Render Forward Pass

## Overview
Rendering Pipelines and Passes decompose volume rendering into distinct, sequential logical blocks or stages to manage complexity, optimize resource usage, and enable independent tuning of geometric projection and visual appearance [S1, S3, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from monolithic ray-marching or single-pass splatting implementations by explicitly separating traversal, shading, and compositing into reusable passes, allowing for techniques like deferred shading and fragment-list accumulation [S3, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized [S1, S3, S4, unofficial].

1.  **Primitive Representation:** The volume is decomposed into primitives. These may be explicit geometric shapes (cubes, cells, splats) or implicit functions sampled via texture hardware [S1, S3, S4, unofficial]. Each primitive $k$ is defined by its position $\mathbf{p}_k$, density/extinction coefficient $g_k$ or $\rho_k$, and a reconstruction kernel $h$ (typically a Gaussian) [S1, unofficial][S6, unofficial][S10, abstract only, unofficial].
2.  **Transformation:** Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., shear-warp) [S2, S3, S4, unofficial]. For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., EWA splatting) to account for foreshortening [S6, unofficial][S10, abstract only, unofficial].
3.  **Rasterization:** The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane. This step leverages hardware-accelerated scan-conversion, depth testing, and blending [S1, S2, S3, S4, unofficial]. The contribution of a voxel $D$ to a screen point $(x,y)$ is determined by the footprint function $F(x,y)$, which is the integral of the 3D kernel along the view direction [S2, unofficial][S6, unofficial][S10, abstract only, unofficial]:
    $$ F(x,y) = \int h(x-x_D, y-y_D, z) \, dz $$
    The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density:
    $$ P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D) $$
    where $\text{weight}(x,y) = F(x-x_D, y-y_D)$ [S10, abstract only, unofficial].
4.  **Compositing:** Contributions are accumulated to form the final image. This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly [S1, S2, S3, unofficial][S7]. Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time) [S10, abstract only, unofficial].
5.  **Hardware Acceleration:** Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Plug-and-Play Ray Marching and Rendering](981-plug-and-play-ray-marching-and-rendering.md)
Provides a modular interface for efficient ray marching and differentiable volumetric rendering, allowing users to plug any user-defined radiance field into a standardized acceleration pipeline. It distinguishes itself from specialized implementations like Instant-NGP by offering a Python API built on PyTorch, which facilitates easier extension to dynamic and unbounded scenes while maintaining high performance.

### [Time-Sliced Pipelined Architecture](1435-time-sliced-pipelined-architecture.md)
A hardware design methodology for volume rendering systems that achieves real-time performance by time-slicing functional blocks to allow the simultaneous processing of multiple tasks. It solves the bottleneck of sequential hardware execution by overlapping pipeline stages, enabling continuous communication between hardware components and software interfaces. Unlike general-purpose DSP-based solutions that require multiple chips for similar volumes, this architecture integrates the entire rendering pipeline into a single system using reusable sub-cores, allowing for efficient layout and configuration based on specific processing requirements.

### [Slice-by-Slice (Sheet Buffer) Splatting](2110-slice-by-slice-sheet-buffer-splatting.md)
A volume rendering optimization that improves image quality over standard "splat-every-sample" compositing by correctly handling visibility through depth-ordered accumulation. It sets itself apart from its parent method, [Splatting](23-splatting.md), by organizing splats into 2D cache-sheets aligned with the volume axis most parallel to the image plane, compositing these sheets slice-by-slice in depth order, and then blending the result into the final image. Unlike [EWA Splatting](1069-ewa-splatting.md), which handles perspective distortion per-splat, this method primarily addresses the "sparkling" artifacts of list-based accumulation by ensuring correct occlusion, though it introduces its own "popping" artifacts if the view angle crosses specific thresholds.

### [Screen Quad Rendering](2435-screen-quad-rendering.md)
The final compositing stage in a multi-pass volume rendering pipeline, responsible for displaying the accumulated volume data (stored in intermediate framebuffers) onto the screen. It solves the problem of transferring rendered results from off-screen render targets to the default framebuffer while allowing for post-processing effects such as cross-section slicing or debug overlays. It differs from sibling methods like [DirectXSplat Renderer API](8504-directxsplat-renderer-api.md) by explicitly separating the volume traversal/compositing logic from the final screen presentation, and from [Plug-and-Play Ray Marching and Rendering](981-plug-and-play-ray-marching-and-rendering.md) by relying on hardware-accelerated rasterization of a fullscreen primitive rather than software-based ray traversal for the final image generation.

### [Rendering Pipeline Architecture](3059-rendering-pipeline-architecture.md)
Refers to the structural organization of volume rendering stages into distinct, sequential logical blocks that process data or image states. It solves the problem of managing complex data transformations by separating geometric projection from visual appearance, allowing for independent optimization of shading, classification, and compositing. It differs from monolithic ray-marching approaches by explicitly decomposing the rendering task into reusable passes, such as attribute accumulation, depth occlusion, and normalization, which can be combined in various configurations like the [Splat Attributes Pass](1066-splat-attributes-pass.md) or the [Three-Pass GPU Point Rendering Pipeline](2837-three-pass-gpu-point-rendering-pipeline.md).

### [Custom Pass Rendering](3629-custom-pass-rendering.md)
A multi-pass, object-order rendering pipeline designed for high-performance visualization of large-scale volumetric data (specifically NanoVDB) and octree-based geometry within a modern graphics API context. It solves the problem of efficiently computing surface attributes (position, normal, material ID) and lighting effects (SSAO, shadows) for sparse volumetric datasets by decoupling geometric traversal from shading. Unlike monolithic ray-marching shaders, this method uses a sequence of specialized FullScreenPass stages to build intermediate G-buffers (hit position, filtered normals, ambient occlusion) before a final shading pass. It is distinct from [Plug-and-Play Ray Marching and Rendering](981-plug-and-play-ray-marching-and-rendering.md) by its explicit separation of traversal and lighting into discrete render passes, and from [Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline](3488-fragment-list-based-rendering-pipeline.md) by its reliance on screen-space fragment buffers rather than explicit primitive lists.

### [DirectXSplat Renderer API](8504-directxsplat-renderer-api.md)
A C++/Direct3D 12 library for rendering 3D Gaussian Splats, providing a rasterization pipeline that handles scene upload, preparation, rendering, and frame submission with explicit resource management. It differs from general-purpose ray marching or CPU-based splitters by offering a host-owned D3D12 architecture where the renderer manages GPU memory residency and LOD culling while the host controls command list recording and queue submission. It is designed for high performance, claiming up to 2.4x faster rendering than `gsplat` in matched-quality benchmarks on NVIDIA hardware.

### [Ray-Centric and Hardware-Accelerated Rendering](8936-ray-centric-and-hardware-accelerated-rendering.md)
Computes the color of each pixel by tracing a ray from the camera through the volume and accumulating contributions from sampled points along the ray path. It differs from object-order splatting by avoiding the sorting and blending overheads required for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel than texture-based splatting [G]. It preserves internal volume information, distinguishing it from isosurface extraction methods like [Marching Cubes](53-marching-cubes.md).

### [Multi-Pass and Sequential Stage Architectures](10539-multi-pass-and-sequential-stage-architectures.md)
Decomposes volume rendering into discrete, ordered processing steps to manage complexity and optimize resource usage. Unlike monolithic ray-marching kernels, this family separates geometric traversal, optical property assignment, and image formation into distinct passes or stages. This separation allows for independent optimization of visual appearance (shading/classification) and geometric projection (compositing), enabling techniques such as deferred shading, fragment-list accumulation, and hybrid light/eye passes that are difficult to achieve in single-pass implementations.

### Image-order Splatting
Uses an image-order approach to improve accuracy when using a perspective projection [S2, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of decomposing rendering into passes is rooted in the evolution of hardware-accelerated graphics. Early splatting methods relied on list-based accumulation, which suffered from sorting overheads and visibility artifacts [S2, unofficial]. The introduction of sheet-buffer and slice-by-slice techniques addressed these by organizing splats into cache-aligned structures [S1, S3]. Modern implementations, such as [DirectXSplat](8504-directxsplat-renderer-api.md) and [Custom Pass Rendering](3629-custom-pass-rendering.md), leverage modern GPU APIs (Direct3D 12, Vulkan/WebGPU) to manage complex multi-pass workflows efficiently [S1, S2, unofficial]. The [Time-Sliced Pipelined Architecture](1435-time-sliced-pipelined-architecture.md) represents an earlier hardware-centric approach to parallelizing these stages [S1, unofficial].
